source_text: Ἰγνάτιος, ὁ καὶ Θεοφόρος, ἐκκλησίᾳ θεοῦ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ ἠγαπημένου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ἠλεημένῃ ἐν παντὶ χαρίσματι, πεπληρωμένῃ ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀγάπῃ, ἀνυστερήτῳ οὔσῃ παντὸς χαρίσματος, θεοπρεπεστάτῃ καὶ ἁγιοφόρῳ, τῇ οὔσῃ ἐν Σμύρνῃ τῆς Ἀσίας. ἐν ἀμώμῳ πνεύματι καὶ λόγῳ θεοῦ πλεῖστα χαίρειν.
thought_title: Greeting to the Church in Smyrna
orientation: Ignatius opens his letter to the church in Smyrna with a formal greeting, identifying himself and blessing the church.
pass_a_gloss: Ignatius, who is also called God-Bearer, to the church of God the Father and of the beloved Jesus Christ, which has been shown mercy in every gift, which has been filled with faith and love, which is lacking in no gift, most befitting God and bearing holy things, which is in Smyrna of Asia. In a blameless spirit and in the word of God, very many greetings.

choices.why: The name is a title meaning 'God-bearer'; transliterating preserves the proper name while the gloss explains the sense.
The perfect passive participle emphasizes a completed state of having received mercy, matching the perfect tense.

choices.english: which is lacking in no gift
choices.why: The adjective with genitive of lack is rendered literally to preserve the negation and the genitive construction.
rejected: in no way deficient in any gift

choices.why: The superlative adjective describes the church as supremely worthy of God, preserving the superlative force.
The compound adjective means 'carrying holy things', rendered literally to preserve the image of the church as bearer of sacred realities.
The standard epistolary greeting formula is rendered literally, with the superlative adverb 'πλεῖστα' as 'very many'.

pass_b_english: Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the church of God the Father and of the beloved Jesus Christ, which is in Smyrna in Asia. This church has been shown mercy in every gift, has been filled with faith and love, is lacking in no gift, is most befitting God and bearer of holiness. I rejoice greatly in a blameless spirit and in the word of God.

problems.why: Ignatius is not sending greetings but rejoicing greatly; the agency is reversed.
problems.fix: rejoice greatly in a blameless spirit and the word of God

problems.why: The Greek adjective means ‘most holy’ or ‘most befitting God’, not ‘bears holy things’.

edits.old: sends very many greetings in a blameless spirit and in the word of God
edits.new: rejoices greatly in a blameless spirit and in the word of God

edits.old: is most befitting God, and bears holy things
edits.new: is most befitting God and most holy

fixed: Changed 'sends very many greetings' to 'rejoices greatly' because πλεῖστα χαίρειν means 'rejoices greatly', not 'sends greetings'.
Changed 'bears holy things' to 'most holy' because ἁγιοφόρῳ is an adjective meaning 'most holy' or 'most befitting God', not 'bears holy things'.

problems.quote: is most befitting God and most holy
problems.why: ἁγιοφόρῳ means 'bearer of holiness/holy things', not 'most holy'
problems.fix: is most befitting God and bearer of holiness
problems.ruling: Greek ἁγιοφόρῳ = ‘holy‑bearer’, not superlative ‘most holy’; translation adds unwarranted superlative.

edits.old: is most befitting God and most holy
edits.new: is most befitting God and bearer of holiness

fixed: Changed 'most holy' to 'bearer of holiness' because ἁγιοφόρῳ means 'bearing holy things' (ἅγιος + φέρω), not 'most holy'.

problems.why: Same epithet rendered four ways; reader may think these are different titles or people.
problems.fix: Standardize to one spelling, note 'Theophorus' as Greek equivalent.

problems.quote: Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus
problems.why: Same Greek title, one translated and one transliterated; reader may think they differ.
problems.fix: Use 'God-Bearer (Theophorus)' consistently or translate both the same way.

edits.old: Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, rejoices greatly
edits.new: Ignatius, who is also called God-Bearer, rejoices greatly

fixed: Standardized the epithet to 'God-Bearer' in both the English and the literal gloss, since the source uses the same Greek term (Θεοφόρος) and the brief's glossary does not prescribe a transliteration.

last_rejected.quote: This church has been shown mercy
last_rejected.source_quote: ἠλεημένῃ ἐν παντὶ χαρίσματι, πεπληρωμένῃ ἐν πίστει καὶ ἀγάπῃ, ἀνυστερήτῳ οὔσῃ παντὸς χαρίσματος, θεοπρεπεστάτῃ καὶ ἁγιοφόρῳ
last_rejected.why: Four participial descriptors of the church are moved to a separate sentence, losing the Greek's direct address form.
last_rejected.fix: ...to the church... shown mercy in every gift, filled with faith and love, lacking in no gift, most befitting God and holy-bearing, which is in Smyrna in Asia.
last_rejected.ruling: Descriptors are restated in a new sentence; meaning unchanged, only stylistic shift.

polish.changed: Reordered the greeting so the recipient church is identified before the closing blessing, and clarified that the final clause is Ignatius's own rejoicing.

notes.why: Same epithet rendered four ways; reader may think these are different titles or people.
notes.fix: Standardize to one spelling, note 'Theophorus' as Greek equivalent.

notes.quote: Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus
notes.why: Same Greek title, one translated and one transliterated; reader may think they differ.
notes.fix: Use 'God-Bearer (Theophorus)' consistently or translate both the same way.

polish.changed: Standardized the rendering of Ignatius's title as Theophorus so readers can recognize the repeated title, and clarified the sentence structure so the church's attributes read as a natural sequence rather than a string of clauses.

notes.why: Same Greek title (Theophorus) rendered three ways; reader may miss connection.
Same Greek title (Theophoros) applied to Ignatius and to Ephesians; reader may miss the echo.
notes.fix: Note that 'bearers of God' echoes Ignatius's own title.
